ops.old: which represents 22% of all U.S. healthcare spending
ops.new: which accounts for about 18% of all U.S. healthcare spending
ops.claim: Medicaid represents 22% of all US healthcare spending
ops.sources: CMS National Health Expenditure Fact Sheet: Medicaid $931.7B, 18% of NHE in 2024 (also 18% in 2023)

ops.old: covers 90 million people and represents 22% of all U.S. healthcare spending
ops.new: covered about 76 million people together with CHIP at the end of 2025 and accounts for about 18% of all U.S. healthcare spending
ops.claim: Medicaid covers 90 million people and is 22% of US health spending
ops.sources: CMS Medicaid & CHIP monthly enrollment report, December 2025: 75.7M (68.5M Medicaid, 7.2M CHIP); CMS NHE Fact Sheet: Medicaid 18% of NHE in 2024
ops.note: 90M was the pandemic-era peak; spending share overstated.

ops.old: matches state spending at rates ranging from 50% to 90% depending on state per-capita income
ops.new: matches state spending at a regular rate (FMAP) that runs from a 50% floor to about 77% depending on state per-capita income, with a separate 90% match for the ACA expansion population
ops.claim: Federal match ranges 50% to 90% depending on state per-capita income
ops.sources: Social Security Act §1905(b) (FMAP formula, 50% floor, 83% statutory cap); HHS ASPE FY2026 FMAP table (highest regular FMAP ~77%, Mississippi); ACA §2001 (90% expansion match)
ops.note: The 90% rate is the expansion match, not part of the income-based FMAP range.

ops.old: as long as the model operates within specific statutory parameters and is evaluated by CMS’s Office of the Actuary.
ops.new: as long as the model operates within specific statutory parameters; expanding a model nationally additionally requires the CMS Chief Actuary to certify that expansion would not increase net program spending.
ops.claim: CMMI models may bypass rulemaking 'as long as ... evaluated by CMS's Office of the Actuary'
ops.sources: Social Security Act §1115A(b)-(c) (testing authority; expansion requires Chief Actuary certification of no increase in net program spending)
ops.note: OACT certifies expansions; it does not evaluate every model.

ops.old: Models that fail to meet these thresholds are terminated. As of 2025, CMMI has terminated 14 models for insufficient evidence of savings or quality improvement, a track record that reflects honest evaluation but has also generated criticism from providers who invested substantially in model infrastructure before termination decisions.
ops.new: Models that fail to meet these thresholds can be modified or terminated. CMMI's own 2021 strategy review found that only six of its more than 50 models had produced statistically significant savings, and in March 2025 it announced it would end four models early, effective December 31, 2025 — Primary Care First, Making Care Primary, ESRD Treatment Choices, and the Maryland Total Cost of Care Model — citing evaluations and forecasts of increased spending; it is a record that reflects honest evaluation but has also drawn criticism from providers who invested substantially in model infrastructure before termination decisions.
ops.claim: As of 2025 CMMI has terminated 14 models for insufficient evidence
ops.sources: CMS Innovation Center Strategy Refresh white paper (Oct 2021): 6 of 50+ models with significant savings; CMS announcement 2025-03-12 (Winston & Strawn / Hogan Lovells client alerts): Primary Care First, Making Care Primary, ESRD Treatment Choices, Maryland TCOC terminated effective 2025-12-31, ~$750M projected savings
ops.note: No source for '14 models'; replaced with documented facts.

ops.old: — Dr. Rahul Rajkumar, former CMMI Deputy Director, Health Affairs Blog, 2024.
ops.claim: Pull-quote attributed to Dr. Rahul Rajkumar, former CMMI Deputy Director, Health Affairs Blog, 2024
ops.sources: Searched Health Affairs Forefront and the web for the quoted text and for a 2024 Rajkumar post; no match
ops.note: Attribution removed; the pull-quote remains as unattributed editorial text (same treatment as Module 3's Dafny/McClellan quotes in phase 6).

ops.old: quality (45% weight), promoting interoperability (25%), improvement activities (15%), and cost (15%).
ops.new: quality (30% weight), cost (30%), promoting interoperability (25%), and improvement activities (15%) — the weights in effect since the 2022 performance year.
ops.claim: MIPS weights quality 45%, PI 25%, IA 15%, cost 15%
ops.sources: CMS Quality Payment Program, MIPS performance category weights (2022 onward: quality 30, cost 30, PI 25, IA 15); 42 CFR 414.1380
ops.note: 45/15 were the 2019 weights.

ops.old: Physicians who generate a sufficient share of their Medicare revenue through APM participation receive a 5% lump-sum bonus payment and are exempt from MIPS reporting requirements
ops.new: Physicians who generate a sufficient share of their Medicare revenue through APM participation become Qualifying APM Participants — originally earning a 5% lump-sum bonus (since reduced and, for 2025 performance onward, lapsed) and a higher fee-schedule update — and are exempt from MIPS reporting requirements
ops.claim: Advanced APM QPs receive a 5% lump-sum bonus
ops.sources: CMS QPP APM Incentive Payment page and CY2026 PFS final rule: 5% (through 2022 performance), 3.5% (2023), 1.88% (2024), none from 2025 performance; 0.75% vs 0.25% conversion-factor update from 2026
ops.note: Stale; consistent with the module's own table and blk013.

ops.old: The CMS data consistently shows that the cost of MIPS compliance for small and independent practices averages $12,800 per physician per year in staff time and technology costs.
ops.new: A 2021 study of independent practices by Khullar and colleagues (JAMA Health Forum) put the cost of MIPS participation at $12,811 per physician per year in 2019, driven by about 200 hours of physician and staff time.
ops.claim: 'CMS data consistently shows' MIPS compliance costs ~$12,800 per physician per year
ops.sources: Khullar D et al., 'Time and Financial Costs for Physician Practices to Participate in the Medicare Merit-based Incentive Payment System,' JAMA Health Forum, May 2021 ($12,811 per physician; 201.7 hours per physician)
ops.note: Figure is real but comes from an independent study, not CMS data.

ops.old: In November 2020, CMS and the Department of Justice’s Office of Inspector General simultaneously published new rules
ops.new: In November 2020, CMS (for the Stark Law) and the HHS Office of Inspector General (for the Anti-Kickback Statute) simultaneously published new rules
ops.claim: 'Department of Justice's Office of Inspector General' issued the AKS rule
ops.sources: HHS OIG final rule 'Revisions to Safe Harbors Under the Anti-Kickback Statute' (85 FR 77684, Dec 2, 2020); CMS final rule 'Modernizing and Clarifying the Physician Self-Referral Regulations' (85 FR 77492)
ops.note: The AKS rule was issued by HHS OIG, not DOJ.

ops.old: As of 2025, 41 states operate Medicaid managed care programs covering at least some beneficiary populations, and 24 states have active Section 1115 waivers that include VBC-oriented payment reform components.
ops.new: As of 2025, 41 states (including DC) contract with comprehensive Medicaid managed care organizations, and many states use Section 1115 waivers to add VBC-oriented payment reform components.
ops.claim: 24 states have active 1115 waivers with VBC payment reform components
ops.sources: KFF Medicaid managed care market tracker (41 states incl. DC with comprehensive MCOs); no source located for '24 states'
ops.note: 41 kept (verified); 24 dropped.

ops.old: MassHealth ACO Program — full-risk global budget ACOs
ops.new: MassHealth ACO Program — Accountable Care Partnership Plans take full capitated risk; Primary Care ACOs take shared risk without insurance risk
ops.claim: MassHealth ACO Program = full-risk global budget ACOs
ops.sources: MassHealth All Provider Bulletin 272 and ACO Models Q&A (mass.gov)
ops.note: Only one of the ACO models carries full risk.

ops.old: Pilots in 5 regions covering food, housing, transportation
ops.new: Pilots in 3 regions covering food, housing, transportation, interpersonal safety; services paused July 1, 2025 when state funding lapsed
ops.claim: NC Healthy Opportunities Pilots in 5 regions
ops.sources: NC DHHS / health plan notice 'Stopping Healthy Opportunities Pilots Services' (effective 2025-07-01); Duke-Margolis / Milbank 'Community Voices from North Carolina's Healthy Opportunities Pilots' (three predominantly rural regions)
ops.note: Three regions, not five; pause added.

ops.old: The CMS All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development Model, known as AHEAD, launched in 2023 and represents
ops.new: The CMS AHEAD Model — announced in 2023 as the States Advancing All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development Model and renamed Achieving Healthcare Efficiency through Accountable Design after CMS redesigned it in September 2025 — represents
ops.claim: AHEAD = 'All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development Model', launched 2023
ops.sources: CMS press release 2023-09-05 (States Advancing AHEAD); CMS AHEAD model page and Innovation Insight on the September 2025 changes (Achieving Healthcare Efficiency through Accountable Design)
ops.note: Name was wrong and is out of date.

ops.old: similar to the model Maryland has operated since 1977 under a waiver from standard Medicare payment rules.
ops.new: similar to the all-payer hospital global budgets Maryland has operated statewide since 2014, built on the all-payer rate-setting system it has run under a Medicare waiver since 1977.
ops.claim: Maryland has operated hospital global budgets since 1977
ops.sources: Maryland HSCRC history; CMS Maryland All-Payer Model (2014-2018) page: rate setting under a 1977 Medicare waiver, global budgets from 2014
ops.note: 1977 is rate setting; global budgets began 2014.

ops.old: And the Health Equity Plan requires each participating state to establish specific, measurable goals for reducing health outcome disparities across racial, ethnic, geographic, and socioeconomic dimensions, with CMS oversight of progress toward those goals as a condition of continued model participation.
ops.new: And population health accountability — originally a state Health Equity Plan with disparity-reduction goals — was replaced in CMS's September 2025 redesign by statewide and hospital Population Health Accountability Plans focused on preventive care and chronic disease prevention, while the requirements to report quality by race and ethnicity and to submit demographic data were dropped and states must now adopt at least two policies promoting choice and competition.
ops.claim: AHEAD's Health Equity Plan requires measurable disparity-reduction goals as a condition of participation
ops.sources: CMS, 'AHEAD Overview' fall 2025 slides (cms.gov/priorities/innovation/files/ahead-overview-fall2025-slides.pdf): PHAPs replace prior plan; states no longer required to report quality metrics by race/ethnicity; hospitals/providers no longer submit demographic data; AHA News 2025-09-03
ops.note: Stale after the September 2025 redesign.

ops.old: and where health equity is a contractual obligation rather than an aspiration.
ops.new: and where population health is a contractual obligation rather than an aspiration.
ops.claim: Pull-quote: under AHEAD 'health equity is a contractual obligation'
ops.sources: As above (AHEAD fall 2025 slides)
ops.note: No longer true after the 2025 redesign; editorial text aligned.

ops.old: The global budgets that Maryland hospitals operate under are legal because of a 47-year-old CMS waiver.
ops.new: The global budgets that Maryland hospitals operate under rest on the state’s all-payer rate-setting authority, first granted by a Medicare waiver in 1977 and continued today under its AHEAD agreement.
ops.claim: Maryland global budgets legal because of a '47-year-old CMS waiver'
ops.sources: CMS AHEAD page (Maryland Cohort 1 from January 2026; agreement signed 2025-11-13 per CMS Innovation Insight); HSCRC history (1977 waiver)
ops.note: Age was wrong for 2026 and the waiver has been superseded by successive model agreements.

ops.old: If no, note that CMS's September 2025 redesign of AHEAD announced no further cohorts; the existing cohorts run through December 31, 2035.
ops.new: If no, note that CMS's September 2025 redesign of AHEAD offered an opportunity for two additional states to participate starting in 2028 and/or 2029; all cohorts now run through December 31, 2035.
ops.claim: CMS's September 2025 AHEAD redesign announced no further cohorts
ops.sources: CMS, 'AHEAD Overview' fall 2025 slides: 'Opportunity for two additional states to participate in the model starting in 2028 and/or 2029'; CMS AHEAD page: 5 states, all cohorts through 2035-12-31
ops.note: Settles the Module 2 vs AHEAD-analysis contradiction from CMS's own materials: new states WERE invited.
